extracted.intended_audience: naturalists/geologists and educated general readers interested in coral reefs and earth-movement theory
extracted.subtask_description: Explain and evaluate theories for the origin, structure, and distribution of coral reefs (atolls, barrier-reefs, fringing-reefs), using observational evidence to test subsidence/uplift hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of the three great classes
rubrics_metrics.description: No theory on the formation of coral-reefs can be considered satisfactory which does not include the three great classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The three classes named and treated are Atolls (lagoon-islands), Barrier-reefs (encircling or fronting shores separated by a broad and rather deep channel), and Fringing-reefs (close attachment to shores). A satisfactory theory must explain all three types and their similarities and differences in structure, grouping, and arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum depth for reef-building corals
rubrics_metrics.description: The utmost depth at which corals can construct reefs is between 20 and 30 fathoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limit is supported by soundings (e.g., prepared tallow on leads showing impressions of living corals up to ~10 fathoms and diminishing with depth) and is central to inferring the necessary depth of any foundation for reefs and to rejecting theories that require coral growth at much greater depths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of a foundation within coral growth depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Reef-building corals, which cannot live at great depths, must have based their massive structures on foundations lying within the requisite depth (20–30 fathoms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where large areas of coral islands exist with no land rising above wave-thrown fragments, it is inferred that foundations originally existed within this limited depth; theories must account for how such foundations were present (not by improbable sediment banks or uniform uplift to that narrow level).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsidence as the explanatory mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: As mountain after mountain, and island after island, slowly sank beneath the water, fresh bases would be successively afforded for the growth of the corals, allowing reefs to build upwards while the land subsided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theory should explain barrier-reefs and atolls as the upward growth of corals during slow subsidence of the underlying land; diagrams/sections showing reefs preserving their form while islands sink are part of the explanatory apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple empirical observations to support subsidence/uplift
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical evidence such as soundings, impressions on lead, deep lagoon channels, undermined trees and posts, recorded earthquakes, upraised organic remains, and submerged dead reefs must be marshalled to infer subsidence or elevation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: undermined cocoa-nut trees and foundation-posts at Keeling, deep lagoon channels with little alluvial accumulation at Vanikoro, uniform depths of dead submerged reefs in the Chagos group (6–8 fathoms) suggesting uniform downward movement. A convincing theory synthesizes such observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain geographic distribution and mapping patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: A valid theory must account for the large-scale geographic distribution of reef types (elongated areas of atolls and barriers vs. lines of fringed coasts) as seen on maps and the grouping/parallel arrangements of atolls relative to island and coastline strike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin's coloured map (atolls dark-blue, barrier-reefs pale-blue, fringing reefs red) shows pale/dark-blue (subsiding areas) near each other and red (uplifted/stationary) areas elsewhere; theory should explain these spatial patterns and alternations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation with volcanic activity and elevation history
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence or absence of active volcanos correlates with areas of uplift or subsidence: active volcanos tend to be in upraised or stationary areas, and are notably absent from the great subsiding areas occupied by atolls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A satisfactory account should reconcile reef distribution with volcanic chains and with evidence of recent elevation (upraised organic remains) to support the inference that areas colored red (fringing/upraised) and blue (barrier/atoll/subsiding) reflect different vertical movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for local structural details and exceptional cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Theory must explain local features such as breaches/passages through reefs facing valleys, imperfect or broken parts of barriers, atolls tied together or divided, and complex forms like the northern Maldiva atolls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms include sediment washed from rivulets killing corals (creating gateways that persist when uplift/subsidence occurs), oceanic and tidal currents preventing rim re-union after breaches, and differential growth or destruction due to food supply, predation, sediment, or loose bottoms. Examples: New Caledonia's imperfect barrier, Maldiva bifurcating channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain reef life-cycle, rates and timescales of change
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsidence must be gradual enough to permit corals to grow upward, and theory should allow for recurrent or intermittent subsidence enabling reefs to keep pace or become submerged and die.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accounts should address how reefs can become very thick over long periods, how dead/submerged reefs ("half-drowned atolls") occur, and why new atolls form in new areas of subsidence without producing an indefinite accumulation of reef mass in older areas (destruction and obliteration occur).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence of fringing-reef width on submarine shore slope and foundation depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Fringing-reef width correlates with how the land slopes under water: narrow (a few yards) where land plunges steeply, wider (up to a mile) where the submarine slope is gentle, extending only until a foundation lies within 20–30 fathoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soundings outside reefs showing gentle submarine inclinations support this; the reef extends only to where the required base depth exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outer-edge growth vigor and sediment impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Corals grow more vigorously and form the highest parts at the outside (exposed to the open sea); sediment washed inwards is harmful and produces a shallow sandy channel between reef and land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why the outer margin is often wall-like and why inner lagoon regions have delicately-branching corals and accumulations of sand; it also explains the tendency for leeward sides to show dead or submerged portions due to sediment transport.
